Caterina Sforza, later known as the “Tigress of Forlì”, was one of the most formidable figures of late medieval Italy. Born into the powerful Sforza family, she rose to dominate the ruthless world of 15th-century Italian politics, where alliances shifted as quickly as daggers were drawn.
At the height of her power, Caterina ruled multiple territories, navigated the dangerous intrigues of papal courts, and personally led her forces during brutal sieges. But her story doesn’t end on the battlefield. She was also a scholar and experimenter, delving into alchemy, medicine, botany, and even early cosmetics, recording her findings in detailed writings that blurred the line between science and legend.

snippet.title: Korean War Every Day (1950–1953)
snippet.description:
The Korean War (1950–1953) stands as one of the most dramatic 
chapters of the Cold War. From North Korea's surprise invasion 
across the 38th parallel, to the UN counteroffensive, China's 
intervention, and the final armistice, this animated map traces 
every key shift on the frontlines.

Often called "The Forgotten War," its consequences shaped 
the Korean Peninsula to this very day.

snippet.title: The Battle that Saved Taiwan - Kinmen Island 1949
snippet.description:
Support the creation of more videos: https://www.patreon.com/historigraph 
Buy a Poster! https://historigraph.media/store

In October 1949, Communist forces launched an amphibious assault on Kinmen Island, expecting an easy victory as the Chinese Civil War drew to a close. Instead, their fishing-boat invasion ran straight into a heavily reinforced Nationalist defence, triggering a chaotic battle that ended in disaster for the attackers.

This video explores the Battle of Kinmen (Guningtou) — the failed PLA landing, the decisive Nationalist counterattack, and how this little-known battle helped prevent an invasion of Taiwan and reshaped US support for Chiang Kai-shek. One of the most important — and overlooked — amphibious failures of the 20th century.

snippet.title: The Lombards - Germanics Conquered the Roman Heartland
snippet.description:
🎥 Watch 300+ exclusive videos on ✔ youtube ► https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCMmaBzfCCwZ2KqaBJjkj0fw/join and ✔ Patreon ► https://www.patreon.com/kingsandgenerals

Kings and Generals animated historical documentary series on the history of medieval period and Franks continues with a video on how the history of the Lombards. Before Lombardy became a region of Italy, the Lombards were a roaming warrior people whose origin story mixed myth, migration, politics, and war. This video follows their rise from the legendary “long-beards” of the Winnils to one of the most important Germanic kingdoms of the early Middle Ages. We trace how a small tribal coalition entered Roman records, settled in Pannonia, fought the Heruli and Gepids, and served the Eastern Roman Empire before turning against it. Under King Alboin, the Lombards invaded a devastated Italy in 568, seized Milan and Pavia, and carved out a kingdom among the ruins of Rome. But conquest brought instability: murder, autonomous dukes, Byzantine resistance, religious change, and a society built around warriors, law, honour, and hierarchy. The story then turns to the 8th century, when Lombard expansion threatened Rome itself, forcing the Pope to seek protection from the rising Carolingian Franks. From Alboin’s bloody legend to Pippin’s invasions and the birth of the Papal States, this is the story of how the Lombards reshaped Italy—and why their kingdom could not survive Frankish power. It is a transformation story linking Rome’s collapse, barbarian migration, medieval state-building, and the rise of Charlemagne’s world in medieval Europe.

snippet.title: Why wasn't Japan allowed to keep Taiwan after WW2? (Short Animated Documentary)
snippet.description:
After losing the Second World War, the Empire of Japan was stripped of its empire, losing everything it had gained since 1895 (and more). Part of this reckoning included the loss of Japanese Formosa, known nowadays as Taiwan. Whilst this had been agreed upon by the UK and USA, whether or not they really wanted it to go to China isn't entirely clear and there were some that even believed Japan shouldn't lose it at all. And so given this ambiguity, why did Japan end up losing Taiwan in 1945 and did the allies try to or want to do anything about it? To find out watch this short and simple animated history documentary.

Think you can name one European country Vikings didn’t conquer?

6 million Europeans today carry Viking DNA, more than the population of six US states combined. Most have no idea their ancestors were Norse warriors. This is the story of the most successful invasion in history: one so complete that it became invisible.

From Ireland to Russia, Sicily to Constantinople, Vikings didn’t just raid—they stayed, ruled, and built. They founded Dublin, created Normandy, conquered England in ONE day, and discovered America 500 years before Columbus. The craziest part is you use Viking words every day, live by their calendar, and might even have their DNA without knowing it.

snippet.title: The Genius Design Behind Star Fort Defenses - Origins of the US Anthem
snippet.description:
🎥 Watch 300+ exclusive videos on ✔ youtube ► https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCMmaBzfCCwZ2KqaBJjkj0fw/join and ✔ Patreon ► https://www.patreon.com/kingsandgenerals

Kings and Generals animated historical documentary series on early modern warfare where we talk about the evolution of the Star Fort, the genius behind its design and Fort Mchenry. When cannon fire made medieval castles obsolete, European engineers answered with one of the most important military designs in history: the bastion fort. This video traces the rise of the low, angular “star fort,” from Renaissance Italy and the Trace Italienne to the great fortress systems of the Netherlands, Habsburg frontier, and Vauban’s France. We explain why tall walls failed, how angled bastions eliminated blind spots, and why siege warfare became a deadly contest of mathematics, trenches, artillery, and engineering. Then the story crosses the Atlantic to Baltimore, where Fort McHenry turned European fortress theory into American coastal defence. Built on Whetstone Point to guard Baltimore Harbor, its pentagonal bastions, dry moat, glacis, and heavy guns faced their defining test during the War of 1812. After burning Washington, the British fleet bombarded Fort McHenry for 25 hours, but the fort held, the flag still flew, and Francis Scott Key found the image that became The Star-Spangled Banner. From Italian city-states to the Chesapeake, this is the story of how star forts changed warfare—and how one American bastion became a national symbol of resistance, engineering, and survival under fire, remembered long after the guns fell silent in 1814 and beyond forever.
